title: The guest is god
hookLine: atithi devo bhava: why Hindu homes treat a surprise guest like family, and where the line comes from
carry: mother, father, teacher, guest: honor each as god

cards: Fly into India and you may well see three Sanskrit words on a poster: atithi devo bhava. The guest is god.
India's tourism posters have used them, and you can find the same words, or their neighbors, framed on kitchen walls. They're much older than any poster.
They come from the same graduation speech as yesterday, the next part of the teacher's charge, and the guest isn't even first on the list.

teach.b: Here's the list, in order. Matri devo bhava. Pitri devo bhava.
Acharya devo bhava. Atithi devo bhava. Mother first, then father, then teacher, then guest.
The grammar is lovely. It isn't quite treat your mother like a god.

teach.h: BE ONE FOR WHOM THE MOTHER IS GOD.
teach.b: It's be someone for whom the mother is a god. It's describing the kind of person the student is leaving to become. And notice who's on it.
Two people who gave you life. One who gave you learning. And then a stranger at the door.
Tradition explains atithi as someone who comes without a set day, unannounced, and they go on the same list as your parents. Then, right after, the teacher turns to giving.
Give with faith; don't give without faith. Give generously. Give with modesty.
Give with a little awe, worried it's not enough. Give with understanding. Five ways to hand something over, and not one of them is give when you feel like it.
Does as god mean obey without question? The charge itself answers that. In the very next breath, the same teacher says: follow our blameless deeds, not the others.
Honor isn't blind. Hindu families live this out in many ways: touching a parent's or elder's feet for a blessing, a festival day for teachers, guru purnima, and a plate of food for whoever turns up.
The list begins at home and ends at the front door, with whoever happens to be standing there.

how: Many Hindus honor parents and elders by touching their feet for a blessing, honor teachers on Guru Purnima, and treat a guest as a form of the divine, offering food and water first.

o: a guest, one who comes without a set day
an elder whose feet you touch
a teacher who takes in a new student

p: the guest who comes without a set day

s: atithi devo bhava was written for a tourism campaign
it's from the Taittiriya Upanishad's teacher's charge, 1.11.
the list puts the mother first
the charge says to give whenever you feel like it
give with faith, generously, with modesty, with awe, with understanding.

games.q: someone you weren't expecting shows up at the door just as dinner is served. you're a student who took the teacher's charge to heart. what do you do?
games.why: atithi devo bhava: the guest is on the same list as your mother, father and teacher. the charge describes someone who sets another plate.

practice: Let one breath go to your mother, or whoever mothered you, living or gone; then one to your father, or whoever fathered you; then one to a teacher, and one to a guest who once turned up unexpectedly in your life.
If any of these is painful, keep the breath and let the face blur, then rest.

wordCard.voice: Atithi, guest. Mother, father, teacher, and the guest at the door: four for whom the student is charged to be someone who sees them as a god.

orig.note: Sanskrit mātṛ (mother) + deva (god) + bhava (be): be one whose god is the mother.

carryVoice: Your line: mother, father, teacher, guest, honor each as god. In the charge, honor never means obeying blindly. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2–3 (the four; the ways of giving)
